name: Tomas Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Morning milking at Ridgeway starts at six. Two hundred dairy goats, and goats are cleverer than cows, they'll open a gate if you leave the latch half done. After milking I clean the parlour, feed the kids, the baby goats I mean, and in summer I'm on the hay and lucerne with Gerry, the owner's brother. I'm the newest hand, and I still get kicked more than anyone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up at Ridgeway?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a taxi for thirty years. Around 2024 I watched the driverless cars start testing in the city and I thought, I'm not going to be the last taxi on the rank. So at 56 I sold the cab to clear the loan and asked Gerry's sister, Helen, for work. The pay's poor and the cab loan ate what savings we had, so Mila and I live on her care home wage and mine and not much else. But I jumped before I was pushed, and I'm proud of that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology in the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I've got an AI app I talk to while I'm mucking out. It reminds me which goats are due to kid, it helped me set up a spreadsheet for milk yields, and when Helen wanted labels for her cheese, I had it write ten versions. Helen thinks I'm mad. But she uses the labels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So all that fuss and the robots don't come. Funny, I left the taxi because of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I jumped too early, and laugh at myself. The lads still on the taxi rank would never let me forget it. Online I'd post something like: well, at least the goats needed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be fine. I like the goats more than I liked the taxi. The tools I use now would keep getting a bit better, and I'd keep using them to make myself useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Ridgeway and keep pushing the small things: milk records, cheese labels, maybe an online shop for Helen. I'd ask her for a bit more per hour if the shop works. And I'd learn to do the hoof trimming properly, because I'm still bad at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit silly, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you regret leaving the taxi, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, for the money. Taxi paid better. But I was sitting twelve hours a day, my back was gone, and here I'm outside. If the robots never came, I'd still have chosen goats, I think. Ask me again in February when it's raining sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would an online shop work at a farm like Ridgeway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen makes about forty kilos of goat cheese a week and sells it at two markets. I've asked the app how to set up a simple shop, and it's not hard. If we sold even ten kilos more a week online, that's real money for a farm this size.

S0.say: I'd laugh that I jumped too early and the taxi drivers would never let me forget it. Online I'd post that at least the goats needed me.
S0.think: I'd be fine: I like the goats more than the taxi, and the tools I use would keep getting a bit better. I'd keep using them to be useful.
S0.do: Keeps working at the goat farm and builds on his tools: milk records, cheese labels and an online shop for the owner. Asks for more pay if the shop works and learns hoof trimming properly.
S0.feel: Calm, if a bit silly about jumping early.
S0.quote: Ask me again in February when it's raining sideways.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas left taxi driving early because he saw driverless cars coming, and he's proud he jumped before he was pushed. He uses AI daily and is already making himself useful beyond his junior role. His humour carries him even when the joke is on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I like, actually. This is my kind of picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people: learn the tools now, don't wait. I'd say it at the pub and online, and I'd mean it. But I'd also say government should help the ones who can't, because not everyone's had my luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's good. Ridgeway's small, but there are robot feeders and camera systems that spot a lame goat, and I'd be the one who sets them up. I'd stop being the junior who gets kicked and be the one who knows the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into a drone licence this winter. Drones can check fences and count goats on the hill, and the course isn't too dear. I'd show Helen a robot feeder and a lameness camera, with numbers, and offer to run them. And I'd keep pushing the online shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned money. Can you afford a drone course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. It's a few hundred. I'd sell my old guitar and do extra weekend milking. Mila would roll her eyes, but she'd let me, she's used to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridgeway might be worse off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerry, maybe. He's 61 and does everything by eye. He'd hate a camera telling him which goat is lame. I'd try to make it his idea, if I could.

S1.say: I'd tell people to learn the tools now and not wait, but also that government should help those who can't. Not everyone has had my luck.
S1.think: For me it's good: I'd set up robot feeders and lameness cameras and become the one who knows the machines, not the junior who gets kicked.
S1.do: Takes a drone licence course this winter, paying by selling a guitar and doing extra weekend milking. Shows the owner costed plans for a robot feeder and lameness camera and offers to run them.
S1.feel: Excited, with some nerves about money.
S1.quote: I'd stop being the junior who gets kicked and be the one who knows the machines.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas sees slow change as his promotion. He's comfortable with risk even with thin savings and would sell his guitar for a drone course. He was thoughtful about the older colleague who'd resent the cameras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's faster than I'd like, even me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is it, everyone needs to move now, and the government needs to make sure people have something to live on. I'm not a big government man, but there'd be no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my plan is to be the one who runs the machines, but if they can do almost anything, they can run themselves. So I'd have maybe a year of being the clever one before I'm not needed either. I'm 60 then and there's nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go round every small farm in the valley this year and offer to set up their machines for a fee, while there's still money in it. I'd cut what we spend, no holidays, nothing new. And I'd talk to my son, he works in IT support, about what jobs are left once it's all automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd have a plan by Friday. That's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd have a plan by Friday. Is that true, or is it what you tell yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. When I sold the cab, I panicked for a week, then I made a list. I'd panic for a week again. Mila would see the panicking part, nobody else would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does only two years' warning change things, compared with more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, all I can do is grab the short money, the set-up jobs, and cut. With five or ten, I could build something that lasts until I'm 66. Two years and it's a sprint at 60, with no money in the bank, and I've got the knees of a taxi driver.

S2.say: I'd say everyone needs to move now and government must make sure people have something to live on. I'm not a big government man, but there'd be no choice.
S2.think: My plan was to run the machines, but if they can do almost anything they'll run themselves. I'd have a year of being useful at 60 with nothing saved.
S2.do: Goes round small farms in the valley offering paid machine set-up while there's money in it. Cuts holidays and spending, and asks his son in IT support which jobs will be left.
S2.feel: Scared but sure he'd have a plan by Friday.
S2.quote: Two years and it's a sprint at 60, with no money in the bank, and I've got the knees of a taxi driver.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI broke Tomas's plan of being the one who runs the machines, and he saw it straight away. He admitted the 'plan by Friday' confidence comes after a private week of panic that only his wife sees. He'd chase short-term money while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: learn it now, and government needs to help people who can't. Five years is enough to train a lot of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is about right. I'd be the drone and robot man in the valley for four years, maybe, and then near enough to 66 that I could slow down. It's still a gamble, but I like those odds better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence first, then a short course on farm robots, and start offering my services to the farms around Ridgeway on weekends. Every bit of that money would go into savings. I'd keep the AI app close, it's how I learn everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mila say about you starting a business at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Tomas, you're not 30. And she'd be right. But she'd also say, go on then, because she knows I'm worse when I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the robots can fix each other. Right now they need a man with a van. When they don't, I'll know my business has a year left.

S3.say: I'd keep telling people to learn the tools now, and that government needs to help those who can't. Five years is enough to train a lot of people.
S3.think: Five years is about right: I'd be the valley's drone and robot man for four years, then close to my pension. It's a gamble, but better odds.
S3.do: Gets a drone licence, then a short course on farm robots, and offers weekend services to farms near Ridgeway. Saves every bit of that extra money and keeps using his AI app to learn.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: Right now they need a man with a van. When they don't, I'll know my business has a year left.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Tomas enough runway for a side business that could take him close to his pension. He knows exactly when it ends, when the machines can fix each other. His wife's support matters, even if she'd tease him about his age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68. That one's almost a gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a great chance if we use the time well, and I'd say it to everyone. Learn now, plan now, help the ones who can't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the best of the three. I'd have years to be useful with the machines, build a little business, and still retire before it all goes automatic. I'd worry for my grandchildren more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence, the robot course, help Ridgeway bring in machines step by step and become the person who runs them. I'd build up the weekend business slowly and save. And I'd keep learning, every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite looking forward to it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any worries at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money, always. If something goes wrong with my health, there's nothing to fall back on. And my granddaughter's 6, she'll be 16 when it arrives, and I wouldn't know what to tell her to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell her, if you had to guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be the kind of person who's not scared of new things. That's the only thing I've got that's worked. I've changed jobs twice and both times it was being curious that saved me.

S4.say: I'd say this is a great chance if we use the time well: learn now, plan now and help those who can't keep up.
S4.think: It's the best of the three for me: years to be useful with machines and build a small business, and I'd retire before it all goes automatic.
S4.do: Takes the drone and robot courses and helps the farm bring in machines step by step, running them himself. Builds a weekend business slowly and saves.
S4.feel: Calm, even looking forward to it.
S4.quote: I've changed jobs twice and both times it was being curious that saved me.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is almost a gift to Tomas: time to use his curiosity and retire before full automation. His only real worries are his health with no savings and what to tell his granddaughter. Curiosity is his whole answer to change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to turn being curious into anything. What would help is cheap or free short courses for older people, a drone licence, a robot course, and a bit of money while you train, so a man with nothing saved can still try.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who'd hire a 60-year-old to set up their robots. Nobody asks that. The answer is small farms, if you're cheap and you turn up on time.

headlineQuote: I jumped before I was pushed, and I'm proud of that.
portrait: Tomas Petrov is 58 and left thirty years of taxi driving after watching driverless cars test in the city; he now milks and feeds goats at Ridgeway, a small goat dairy and hay farm. He's the newest hand and gets kicked the most, but uses an AI app every day and already handles the farm's records and cheese labels. He's pragmatic about politics and comfortable with risk, even though the cab loan wiped out his savings. Slow change and ten-year AGI excite him as chances to become the valley's drone and robot man. Two-year AGI scares him because there'd be no time to build anything before he's 60.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to turn his curiosity into work that lasts.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free short courses for older workers, like drone and farm robot training, with some money to live on while training.
